--- format: revealjs-clean: css: misc/slides.css smaller: true execute: cache: true --- ::: {.cell} ::: # Sentinel Data
Types, Signatures & Preprocessing {.r-fit-text .titlepage} ## Learning Objectives {.smaller} By the end of this lesson you will be able to: - Explain GDAL **data types** and choose the right type for a given value range - Use **scale and offset** to store data compactly without loss of meaningful precision - Navigate the **Sentinel-2 SAFE format** and import bands in R - Convert raw **Digital Numbers (DN)** to surface reflectance values - Apply the **SCL band** to mask clouds and produce a cloud-free image - Apply a **data pipeline** from download to analysis-ready raster # Data Types, scale and offset {#sec-data-types .subtitle} ## Why this matters - Storage space! - Sentinel-2 bands are stored as **raw integers** (UInt16, values ~0–15000) - The conversion to surface reflectance requires a **scale and offset** — documented in a separate XML file - GDAL reads individual JP2 files, not the full product → **the conversion is never applied automatically** - To work with S2 data correctly, we need to understand what scale and offset are and how to apply them :::{.notes} - ESA's design assumes the full SAFE product is used with their toolchain (SNAP, Sen2Cor) — scale/offset lives at the product level (MTD_MSIL2A.xml), not the file level - GDAL reads files, not products — so there is no mechanism for it to auto-apply the conversion - This is the motivating problem for this entire section ::: ## Raster data types - Raster data is always stored as **numeric** - GDAL defines the supported types — shared by R, Python, QGIS - In memory: R/Python types; on disk: GDAL types - Choice of type affects **file size** and **precision** ## Raster data types {.smaller} :::{#tbl-datatypes} | Data type | Minimum | Maximum | Size[^1]| Factor | |-------------------|---------------:|--------------:|--------:|-------:| | Byte | 0 | 255 | 39M | 1x | | UInt16 | 0 | 65,535 | 78M | 2x | | Int16, CInt16 | -32,768 | 32,767 | 78M | 2x | | UInt32 | 0 | 4,294,967,295 | 155M | ~4x | | Int32, CInt32 | -2,147,483,648 | 2,147,483,647 | 155M | ~4x | | Float32, CFloat32 | -3.4E38 | 3.4E38 | 155M | ~4x | | Float64, CFloat64 | -1.79E308 | 1.79E308 | 309M | ~8x | : The possible ranges of different datatypes in `gdal` (source: @amatulli2024) [^1]: Difference in file size using constant dataset (same values and resolution) and varying the datatype ::: :::{.notes} - If you store categorical data, use integer datatype and store the corespondence in the metadata - Always be minimalistic about which datatype you need. - Question if you have a continuous value from 0 to 1, which datatype do you use? - Not `Float32`! But Multiply by 100 and use `Byte` or by 1000 (if you need more precision) and use `UInt16` - Question: if you are measuring temperature, and your values are floating point ranging is -20 to +40 degrees, what datatype are you going to use? - Not CFloat32! - Multiply by 100 and use `CInt16` - Question: if you compute NDVI and have values in the range 0 - 1, what datatype do you use? - Not `Float32`, but not `CInt16` either: - Transform the values to 0 - 255 ::: ## Choosing a data type - Naively: value range determines the datatype - Better: **transform values** to fit a smaller type - Example: NDVI ∈ [−1, 1] → rescale to [0, 255] → store as `Byte` ## Rescaling / Transforming values Min-max normalization maps any range $[\min(x), \max(x)]$ to a target range $[a, b]$: $$x' = a + \frac{(x-\min(x))\times(b - a)}{\max(x)-\min(x)}$$ For NDVI ∈ [−1, 1] rescaled to [0, 255]: - $x$ — measured value, $x'$ — stored value - $a = 0$, $b = 255$ — target range - $\min(x) = -1$, $\max(x) = 1$ --- - We can use these values and simplify the formula as follows: \begin{align} x' &= 0 + \frac{(x+1)\times 255}{2} \\ x' &= \frac{255x+255}{2} \\ x' &= 127.5x+127.5 \\ \end{align} - Formula: $x' = 127.5x + 127.5$ - Example: NDVI $0.2$ → stored as $153$ - Two parameters describe the rescaling: - $x' = x \times \underbrace{127.5}_{\text{scale}} + \underbrace{127.5}_{\text{offset}}$ ## Precision (and lack thereof) - Only 255 distinct values → limited precision - Precision = $\frac{1}{\text{scale}} = \frac{1}{127.5} \approx 0.008$ - Every stored NDVI is rounded to the nearest $0.008$ - Is this enough? → depends on the use case ## R Implementation for vectors - `scale_minmax()` applies the formula to a numeric vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scale_minmax <- function( x, a = 0, # the minimum value of the new range (default 0) b = 255 # the maximum value of the new range (default 255) ){ min_x = min(x) max_x = max(x) a + (x - min_x) * (b - a) / (max_x - min_x) } ``` ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ndvi_measured <- runif(10, -1, 1) ndvi_stored <- scale_minmax(ndvi_measured) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Restoring the original values - A colleague receiving your file needs to know how to get back the original values - Invert the transformation using `scale` and `offset`: $$x = \frac{x' - 127.5}{127.5}$$ ## R implementation for rasters - GDAL supports scale/offset natively (pass directly to `writeRaster()`) - Values are stored in file metadata and recognized during import - Formulas to derive them from the value range: \begin{align} \text{scale} &= \frac{b - a}{\max(x)-\min(x)} \\ \\ \text{offset} &= \frac{a \times \max(x) - b \times \min(x)}{\max(x)-\min(x)} \end{align} Note: - $a$ and $b$ refer to the target range - min and max could either be the *theoretical* or *practical* extremes: **What are pros / cons of using either?** --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scoff_params <- function(x, a = 0, b = 255, min_x = min(x), max_x = max(x)) { scale <- (b - a) / (max_x - min_x) offset <- (a * max_x - b * min_x) / (max_x - min_x) c(scale = scale, offset = offset) } scoff_params(ndvi_measured) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` scale offset 127.5 127.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} scoff_params(ndvi_measured, min_x = -1, max_x = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` scale offset 127.5 127.5 ``` ::: ::: ## R implementation for rasters - `scoff_params()` works for vectors, but needs two adjustments for rasters: 1. `min()`/`max()` return per-cell values → use `minmax()` for global min/max 2. `writeRaster()` divides by `scale` and subtracts `offset` → both must be inverted ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scoff_params <- function(x, a = 0, b = 255) { stopifnot(nlyr(x) == 1) mm <- minmax(x)[, 1] scale <- (b - a) / (mm[2] - mm[1]) offset <- (a * mm[2] - b * mm[1]) / (mm[2] - mm[1]) c(scale = 1 / scale, offset = -offset) } ``` ::: ## R implementation for rasters Let's import a raster, calculate the `scale` and `offset` values and use these values to write to disk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} elev <- rast(system.file("ex/elev.tif", package="terra")) so <- scoff_params(elev) writeRaster( elev, "data-out/datatypes/INT1U.tif", overwrite = TRUE, scale = so["scale"], offset = so["offset"] ) ``` ::: ## R implementation for rasters - GDAL embeds `scale` and `offset` in the file metadata - On import, any GDAL-based software restores the original values automatically - The stored `INT1U` bytes are invisible — you always get back the original range ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Lossless Compression - Even after choosing a compact datatype, files can be compressed further - **Lossless** compression reduces file size without changing any pixel values — the original data is perfectly recoverable - GeoTIFF supports several lossless algorithms via GDAL; **DEFLATE** is the most widely used ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} writeRaster(r, "output.tif", gdal = "COMPRESS=DEFLATE") ``` ::: - Compression is transparent to readers: any GDAL-based software (R, QGIS, Python) decompresses automatically on load - Combine datatype + compression for maximum savings: `INT1U + DEFLATE` can be **8× smaller** than uncompressed `FLT8S` :::{.notes} - DEFLATE is identical to the algorithm used in ZIP files — students will have intuition for it - LZW is an older alternative; ZSTD is newer and faster but less universally supported - Lossy compression (JPEG) exists for imagery but is rarely appropriate for analysis — pixel values change, which breaks indices and classification - "Transparent to readers" is the key selling point — no extra steps needed when loading the file ::: # Showcase: Importing Sentinel data {.subtitle} ## Download data To download Sentinel data: 1. Go to the [Copernicus Browser](https://browser.dataspace.copernicus.eu/) website 2. Login using your credentials 3. Go to your area of interest 4. Click on the "Search" Tab in the left panel 5. In Data Source, select *Sentinel 2* → *L2A* 6. Choose your desired time frame 7. Click on the "Search" button 8. From the search results, download one or two scenes ## Copernicus SAFE Format I - Downloaded scenes come as a **SAFE** folder (distributed as `.zip`) - Contains image bands as individual **JP2** files + metadata in XML - Key contents: - `IMG_DATA/` — band images at 10m, 20m, 60m resolution - `GRANULE/` — scene-level data and annotations - `manifest.safe` — general product info ## Copernicus SAFE Format II The SAFE folder above includes the following content: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` levelName 1 data-large 2 °--S2B_MSIL2A_20240915T102559_N0511_R108_T32TMS_20240915T131207.SAFE 3 ¦--DATASTRIP 4 ¦ °--DS_2BPS_20240915T131207_S20240915T102803 5 ¦ ¦--MTD_DS.xml 6 ¦ °--QI_DATA 7 ¦ ¦--FORMAT_CORRECTNESS.xml 8 ¦ ¦--GENERAL_QUALITY.xml 9 ¦ ¦--GEOMETRIC_QUALITY.xml 10 ¦ ¦--RADIOMETRIC_QUALITY.xml 11 ¦ °--SENSOR_QUALITY.xml 12 ¦--GRANULE 13 ¦ °--L2A_T32TMS_A039316_20240915T102803 14 ¦ ¦--AUX_DATA 15 ¦ ¦ ¦--AUX_CAMSFO 16 ¦ ¦ °--AUX_ECMWFT 17 ¦ ¦--IMG_DATA 18 ¦ ¦ ¦--R10m 19 ¦ ¦ ¦ ¦--T32TMS_20240915T102559_AOT_10m.jp2 20 ¦ ¦ ¦ ¦--T32TMS_20240915T102559_B02_10m.jp2 21 ¦ ¦ ¦ °--... (etc) 22 ¦ ¦ ¦--R20m 23 ¦ ¦ ¦ ¦--T32TMS_20240915T102559_AOT_20m.jp2 24 ¦ ¦ ¦ ¦--T32TMS_20240915T102559_B01_20m.jp2 25 ¦ ¦ ¦ °--... (etc) 26 ¦ ¦ °--R60m 27 ¦ ¦ ¦--T32TMS_20240915T102559_AOT_60m.jp2 28 ¦ ¦ ¦--T32TMS_20240915T102559_B01_60m.jp2 29 ¦ ¦ °--... (etc) 30 ¦ ¦--MTD_TL.xml 31 ¦ °--QI_DATA 32 ¦ ¦--FORMAT_CORRECTNESS.xml 33 ¦ ¦--GENERAL_QUALITY.xml 34 ¦ ¦--GEOMETRIC_QUALITY.xml 35 ¦ ¦--L2A_QUALITY.xml 36 ¦ ¦--MSK_CLASSI_B00.jp2 37 ¦ ¦--MSK_CLDPRB_20m.jp2 38 ¦ ¦--MSK_CLDPRB_60m.jp2 39 ¦ ¦--MSK_DETFOO_B01.jp2 40 ¦ ¦--MSK_DETFOO_B02.jp2 41 ¦ ¦--... (etc) 42 ¦ ¦--MSK_QUALIT_B01.jp2 43 ¦ ¦--MSK_QUALIT_B02.jp2 44 ¦ ¦--MSK_SNWPRB_20m.jp2 45 ¦ ¦--MSK_SNWPRB_60m.jp2 46 ¦ ¦--SENSOR_QUALITY.xml 47 ¦ °--T32TMS_20240915T102559_PVI.jp2 48 ¦--HTML 49 ¦ ¦--banner_1.png 50 ¦ ¦--banner_2.png 51 ¦ ¦--banner_3.png 52 ¦ ¦--star_bg.jpg 53 ¦ ¦--UserProduct_index.html 54 ¦ °--UserProduct_index.xsl 55 ¦--INSPIRE.xml 56 ¦--manifest.safe 57 ¦--MTD_MSIL2A.xml 58 ¦--rep_info 59 ¦ ¦--S2_PDI_Level-2A_Datastrip_Metadata.xsd 60 ¦ ¦--S2_PDI_Level-2A_Tile_Metadata.xsd 61 ¦ °--S2_User_Product_Level-2A_Metadata.xsd 62 °--S2B_MSIL2A_20240915T102559_N0511_R108_T32TMS_20240915T131207-ql.jpg ``` ::: ::: --- The bands are in `IMG_DATA/` — one JP2 per band, at 10m, 20m, and 60m. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s2_files <- list.files("data-large/S2B_MSIL2A_20240915T102559_N0511_R108_T32TMS_20240915T131207.SAFE/GRANULE/L2A_T32TMS_A039316_20240915T102803/IMG_DATA/R60m/", "\\.jp2$", full.names = TRUE) ``` ::: - Filter to spectral bands only (`B01`–`B12`) - Extract band names from filenames with `str_split_fixed()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # selecting only the bands we are interested in: s2_files <- s2_files[str_detect(s2_files, "B\\d{2}")] s2 <- rast(s2_files) # Extracting the band names from the file names and adding these names(s2) <- str_split_fixed(names(s2), "_",4)[,3] names(s2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "B01" "B02" "B03" "B04" "B05" "B06" "B07" "B09" "B11" "B12" ``` ::: ::: --- - Test if the data is loaded correctly: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(s2[[1]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: --- - Values range 0–15000 → **not yet reflectance** (see @sec-data-types) - GDAL hasn't applied scale/offset automatically → we must do it manually - The conversion formula is documented in `MTD_MSIL2A.xml`: $$DN = \rho \times Q - O$$ where $Q$ = quantification value and $O$ = radiometric add offset — let's extract them: --- Searching for `QUANTIFICATION_VALUE` in `SAFE/MTD_MSIL2A.xml`: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 10000 1000.0 1000.0 ``` ::: ::: --- Searching for `ADD_OFFSET` in `SAFE/MTD_MSIL2A.xml`: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 -1000 ``` ::: ::: --- - $Q$ = 10'000, $O$ = −1'000 → $\rho = (DN - 1000) / 10000$ - But are the resulting values physically plausible? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s2b <- (s2 - 1000)/10000 minmax(s2b) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` B01 B02 B03 B04 B05 B06 B07 B09 B11 min -0.1000 -0.100 -0.1000 -0.1000 -0.1000 -0.1000 -0.100 -0.100 -0.1000 max 1.8709 1.802 1.7195 1.6616 1.6448 1.6102 1.594 1.573 1.5258 B12 min -0.1000 max 1.5155 ``` ::: ::: ## Out-of-range reflectance values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(s2b) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: - Reflectance is bounded by definition: 0 (no reflection) to 1 (perfect reflection) - Yet the histogram shows values both **below 0** and **above 1** ## Why are values out of range? - **Below 0** — ESA intentionally introduced a −1000 DN offset (processing baseline 04.00) - Dark surfaces (deep water, shadows) can have slightly negative reflectance after atmospheric correction - The offset shifts all DNs up to keep them positive on disk; subtracting it back out exposes those negatives - These values are **physically meaningful** — clipping them to 0 alters real data - **Above 1** — clouds and saturated pixels exceed the calibration reference; these are true artefacts - The proper fix for both is **SCL masking**: clouds (8, 9), shadows (3), and water (6) are flagged and excluded - After masking, residual out-of-range values are rare; clipping is then a safe fallback --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plotRGB(s2b, r = 4, g = 3, b = 2, stretch = "histogram", smooth = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # To export the R,G,B bands to a True Color Geotiff: writeRaster(s2b[[c(4,3,2)]], "data-out/sentinel-rgb.tif", overwrite = TRUE) ``` ::: To calculate NDVI, we can create our custom function and apply it to the `s2b` object using `app`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ndvi <- \(x){(x[5]-x[4])/(x[5]+x[4])} s2_ndvi <- app(s2b, ndvi) s2_ndvi[!is.finite(s2_ndvi)] <- NA tm_shape(s2_ndvi) + tm_raster(style = "cont",midpoint = 0) + tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Cloud Masking with the SCL Band {#sec-cloud-masking .subtitle} ## Why clouds are a problem - Clouds reflect strongly across all bands — a cloudy pixel does **not** represent the surface below - Using cloudy pixels in analysis (e.g. NDVI, classification) introduces severe errors - Sentinel-2 L2A includes a **Scene Classification Layer (SCL)** → per-pixel quality flag generated automatically during atmospheric correction :::{.notes} - Unlike thin haze, which affects values subtly, clouds completely obscure the surface — affected pixels must be excluded, not corrected - The SCL is generated by Sen2Cor (ESA's atmospheric correction processor) using spectral rules and auxiliary data - It is not perfect — thin cirrus and cloud shadows in complex terrain can be misclassified — but it is the standard starting point ::: ## The Scene Classification Layer (SCL) | Value | Class | Keep? | |---|---|---| | 0 | No Data | ✗ | | 1 | Saturated / Defective | ✗ | | 2 | Dark Area Pixels | ✗ | | 3 | Cloud Shadows | ✗ | | 4 | Vegetation | ✓ | | 5 | Bare Soils | ✓ | | 6 | Water | ✓ | | 7 | Unclassified | ~ | | 8 | Cloud, Medium Probability | ✗ | | 9 | Cloud, High Probability | ✗ | | 10 | Thin Cirrus | ✗ | | 11 | Snow or Ice | ✓ | :::{.notes} - Class 7 (Unclassified) is ambiguous — in practice, many workflows discard it to be safe, others keep it - Classes 8 and 9 are the main cloud mask; class 3 (shadow) is equally important and often missed by users - Class 2 (dark area) catches topographic shadows in mountainous terrain — relevant in Swiss scenes ::: ## Importing the SCL band - The SCL band is stored as a separate JP2 file in the `R20m` resolution folder (not `R10m`) - It follows the same naming convention as the spectral bands ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: :::{.notes} - The SCL is only available at 20m and 60m resolution — it must be resampled to match the resolution of the band stack you are masking - `resample(scl, s2b, method = "near")` aligns it to the target grid — nearest-neighbour is correct here because SCL is categorical ::: ## Applying the cloud mask ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # define which SCL classes are valid (cloud-free surface) valid_classes <- c(4, 5, 6, 11) # create a binary mask: TRUE where pixel is valid cloud_mask <- scl %in% valid_classes # apply to the reflectance stack s2_masked <- mask(s2b, cloud_mask, maskvalues = FALSE) # clip residual out-of-range values after masking force_minmax <- \(x, min = 0, max = 1){ x[x < min] <- min; x[x > max] <- max; x } s2_masked <- app(s2_masked, force_minmax) ``` ::: - `%in%` tests membership cell-by-cell and returns a Boolean raster - `mask(..., maskvalues = FALSE)` sets cells to `NA` wherever the mask is `FALSE` (i.e. cloudy) :::{.notes} - Remind students that `mask()` was introduced in Lesson 1 — this is the same function, now applied for a real purpose - The result is a SpatRaster with the same bands as before but NA for all cloudy/shadowed pixels - Depending on cloud cover, this may remove a large portion of the image — this is expected, not an error ::: ## Before and after masking ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Before masking: full scene (RGB)](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![After masking: clouds and shadows set to NA](lesson3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## How much of the image is usable? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # count valid (non-NA) pixels in band 1 as a fraction of total pixels n_total <- ncell(s2_masked) n_valid <- global(!is.na(s2_masked[[1]]), sum)[[1]] cat(sprintf("Valid pixels: %.1f%%\n", 100 * n_valid / n_total)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Valid pixels: 74.6% ``` ::: ::: - If usable coverage is low, consider: - **Choosing a different date** with less cloud cover - **Mosaicking** multiple acquisitions from nearby dates - **Seasonal compositing**: combine all cloud-free pixels from a season into one image :::{.notes} - A common rule of thumb: discard scenes with > 20% cloud cover over your study area - But study area cloud cover matters more than full scene cloud cover — a scene can be 80% cloudy globally but cloud-free over your area of interest - Seasonal composites (e.g. median of all July scenes) are very robust and widely used in land cover mapping ::: ## References {#refs}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
